vulnerabilities.description: Due to incorrect host parsing, applications that rely on UriComponentsBuilder to parse and validate an externally provided URL string may be exposed to a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack. Affected versions: Spring Framework 7.0.0 through 7.0.7; 6.2.0 through 6.2.18.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. No shipped component parses externally provided URLs with UriComponentsBuilder.

ratings.justification: spring-web ships only inside the 5.x license-tracking application, which never parses externally provided URLs with UriComponentsBuilder and makes no outbound HTTP requests.

analysis.detail: The Liquibase CLI ships no Spring web code; spring-web is only an optional, compile-time dependency of liquibase-core and is not bundled. The scanner reports spring-web from the license-tracking application, a separately started Spring Boot service shipped in 5.x and removed in 6.0.0. Docker images 5.0.0 through 5.2.2 carry it as an unextracted archive under /liquibase/dist (liquibase-license-tracking-1.0.0-beta.tar.gz). It runs only if a user extracts and starts it. The application carries Spring Framework 6.2.2 in 5.0.0 to 5.0.2, 6.2.12 in 5.0.3, 7.0.3 in 5.1.0, 7.0.6 in 5.1.1 and 7.0.7 in 5.2.0, all in range, and the fixed 7.0.8 in 5.2.1 and 5.2.2. The advisory applies only to applications that use UriComponentsBuilder to parse and validate an externally provided URL string. A full source review of the application found no use of UriComponentsBuilder, ServletUriComponentsBuilder or any other URI builder, and no HTTP client (RestTemplate, RestClient, WebClient, java.net.URL or HttpClient). Of its three REST controllers, only the license-track one takes input, JSON license-tracking batches whose JDBC URL field is stored and reported as an opaque string and never parsed as a URL or dereferenced; the report and health endpoints take no parameters. The application makes no outbound requests, so no server-side request forgery path exists.

vulnerabilities.description: In Spring Framework, versions 6.0.x as of 6.0.5, versions 6.1.x and 6.2.x, an application is vulnerable to a reflected file download (RFD) attack when it sets a "Content-Disposition" header with a non-ASCII charset, where the filename attribute is derived from user-supplied input. Affected versions: Spring Framework 6.2.0 through 6.2.7; 6.1.0 through 6.1.20; 6.0.5 through 6.0.28.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. No shipped component sets a Content-Disposition header with ContentDisposition.

ratings.justification: spring-web ships only inside the 5.x license-tracking application, which never builds a Content-Disposition header, so the faulty filename encoding is never used.

analysis.detail: The Liquibase CLI ships no Spring web code; spring-web is only an optional, compile-time dependency of liquibase-core and is not bundled. The scanner reports spring-web from the license-tracking application, a separately started Spring Boot service shipped in 5.x and removed in 6.0.0. Docker images 5.0.0 through 5.2.2 carry it as an unextracted archive under /liquibase/dist (liquibase-license-tracking-1.0.0-beta.tar.gz). It runs only if a user extracts and starts it. The application carries Spring Framework 6.2.2 in 5.0.0 to 5.0.2, which is in range; 5.0.3 and later carry 6.2.12 or 7.0.x, which are not affected. The advisory applies only to applications that build a Content-Disposition response header with ContentDisposition.Builder#filename(String, Charset) from unsanitized user input. None of the application's classes references ContentDisposition or sets a Content-Disposition header; its three REST controllers return a health object, a license-tracking batch acknowledgement and a usage report rendered as text, JSON or HTML, never a file download.
